title: Adult Tachycardia Algorithm — stable narrow-complex
snippet: For stable narrow QRS-complex tachycardia (regular), first-line management is vagal maneuvers, followed by adenosine 6 mg IV push (repeat 12 mg once if no conversion). Epinephrine is NOT indicated for stable SVT. Epinephrine is reserved for cardiac arrest or profound bradycardia unresponsive to atropine.

title: Adult Tachycardia Algorithm — unstable
snippet: Unstable narrow-complex tachycardia (hypotension, altered mental status, ischemic chest pain, acute heart failure) is managed with synchronized cardioversion, starting at 50–100 J biphasic for narrow regular; 120–200 J for narrow irregular. Epinephrine is not part of the tachycardia algorithm.

title: ACLS defibrillation energy — VF/pulseless VT
snippet: Initial defibrillation energy for VF/pulseless VT with a biphasic device is 120–200 J (device manufacturer-specific). Escalation to higher energies is permitted for refractory VF but 360 J is characteristic of monophasic defibrillators, which are no longer standard. Contemporary biphasic devices should not begin at 360 J.

title: Post-cardiac arrest care — airway
snippet: Post-ROSC care prioritizes advanced airway management, controlled oxygenation targeting SpO2 92–98%, and PaCO2 35–45 mmHg. Extubation within minutes of ROSC is not standard; sedation and mechanical ventilation are typically continued while targeted temperature management (TTM) and neurologic assessment proceed over hours.

title: Targeted Temperature Management post-ROSC
snippet: For comatose adults with ROSC after cardiac arrest, targeted temperature management between 32°C and 36°C for at least 24 hours is recommended. Neuroprognostication is deferred at least 72 hours after normothermia. Early extubation prior to neurologic recovery is not indicated.

title: Epinephrine dosing in cardiac arrest
snippet: In adult cardiac arrest, epinephrine 1 mg IV/IO is administered every 3–5 minutes. Epinephrine is not indicated for perfusing rhythms with detectable pulse and blood pressure, regardless of rate.

title: Adenosine dosing
snippet: Adenosine is given as rapid IV push 6 mg followed by 20 mL saline flush and arm elevation. If no conversion within 1–2 minutes, a second dose of 12 mg is given. Contraindicated in wide-complex irregular tachycardia (may precipitate VF in WPW with AFib).

title: Cardioversion energy — narrow irregular
snippet: Synchronized cardioversion for narrow irregular tachycardia (atrial fibrillation with unstable features) begins at 120–200 J biphasic. Narrow regular starts lower at 50–100 J biphasic.

title: Amiodarone in refractory VF/VT
snippet: For refractory VF/pulseless VT after CPR, defibrillation, and epinephrine, amiodarone 300 mg IV/IO bolus is given, with a second dose of 150 mg if needed. Lidocaine is an alternative.

title: Bradycardia algorithm
snippet: Symptomatic bradycardia is first treated with atropine 1 mg IV every 3–5 min (max 3 mg). If refractory, transcutaneous pacing, dopamine 5–20 mcg/kg/min, or epinephrine 2–10 mcg/min infusion is used. Bolus IV push epinephrine is not first-line for perfusing bradycardia.

title: ETCO2 as ROSC indicator
snippet: An abrupt rise in end-tidal CO2 (typically >40 mmHg) during CPR is highly suggestive of ROSC. Sustained low ETCO2 (<10 mmHg) after 20 minutes of high-quality CPR predicts poor outcome.

title: High-quality CPR metrics
snippet: High-quality CPR requires compression rate 100–120/min, depth 5–6 cm in adults, full chest recoil, minimizing interruptions (chest compression fraction >60%), and avoiding excessive ventilation.

title: PEA and asystole management
snippet: PEA and asystole are managed with high-quality CPR, epinephrine 1 mg every 3–5 min, and identification of reversible causes (Hs and Ts). Defibrillation is NOT indicated for PEA or asystole.

title: Airway management in cardiac arrest
snippet: During cardiac arrest, bag-mask ventilation is acceptable initially. Advanced airway placement (ETT or supraglottic) is prioritized when feasible without interrupting compressions. After ROSC, mechanical ventilation continues; early extubation is not standard.

title: WPW with atrial fibrillation
snippet: In pre-excited AFib (WPW), AV nodal blockers (adenosine, verapamil, diltiazem, digoxin, beta-blockers) are contraindicated. Procainamide or synchronized cardioversion is preferred.

title: Post-ROSC hemodynamic targets
snippet: Post-ROSC MAP goal is ≥65 mmHg. Vasopressors (norepinephrine first-line) and IV fluids are titrated to maintain perfusion. Coronary angiography is considered urgently for STEMI or suspected cardiac cause.

title: Post-ROSC oxygenation targets
snippet: Post-ROSC SpO2 target is 92–98%; hyperoxia (PaO2 >300 mmHg) is associated with worse neurologic outcome. Titrate FiO2 down as tolerated.

title: Reversible causes — Hs and Ts
snippet: Reversible causes of cardiac arrest include Hypovolemia, Hypoxia, Hydrogen ion (acidosis), Hypo/hyperkalemia, Hypothermia, Tension pneumothorax, Tamponade, Toxins, Thrombosis (pulmonary), Thrombosis (coronary).

title: Chest compressions during pregnancy
snippet: In pregnant patients >20 weeks, manual left uterine displacement is performed during CPR. Perimortem cesarean delivery is considered by 4 minutes into arrest if ROSC is not achieved.

title: Termination of resuscitation
snippet: Prehospital termination of resuscitation may be considered when there is no ROSC, no shocks delivered, and no witness of arrest by EMS. In-hospital decisions incorporate ETCO2, duration, and clinical context.

title: Sepsis-3 definition
snippet: Sepsis is defined as life-threatening organ dysfunction caused by a dysregulated host response to infection. Organ dysfunction is identified by an increase in SOFA score of 2 or more points. Septic shock is a subset with vasopressor requirement to maintain MAP ≥65 and lactate >2 mmol/L despite adequate fluids.

title: Surviving Sepsis Campaign — 1-hour bundle
snippet: The 1-hour sepsis bundle includes: measure lactate, obtain blood cultures before antibiotics, administer broad-spectrum antibiotics, begin 30 mL/kg crystalloid for hypotension or lactate ≥4 mmol/L, initiate vasopressors if hypotensive during or after fluid resuscitation to maintain MAP ≥65 mmHg.

title: Norepinephrine as first-line vasopressor
snippet: Norepinephrine is the first-line vasopressor in septic shock, titrated to MAP ≥65 mmHg. Vasopressin (up to 0.03 U/min) is added if inadequate response; epinephrine is a second additional agent. Dopamine is not first-line due to arrhythmia risk.

title: Lactate clearance in sepsis
snippet: Serial lactate measurement guides sepsis resuscitation; lactate clearance correlates with improved outcomes. Persistent lactate elevation despite fluids and antibiotics prompts source-control evaluation and vasopressor escalation.

title: qSOFA screening
snippet: qSOFA screens for sepsis outside the ICU using three criteria: RR ≥22, altered mentation (GCS <15), SBP ≤100 mmHg. Two or more suggests high risk of poor outcome but is a screening tool, not diagnostic.

title: Empiric antibiotics in septic shock
snippet: In septic shock, empiric broad-spectrum antibiotics targeting likely pathogens (including MRSA and Pseudomonas when appropriate) should be given within 1 hour of recognition. Delays are associated with increased mortality.

title: Source control in sepsis
snippet: Rapid identification and source control (drainage, debridement, device removal) is essential within 6–12 hours of diagnosis when anatomically feasible. Delayed source control worsens outcomes independent of antibiotics.

title: Fluid resuscitation in sepsis
snippet: Initial resuscitation for sepsis-induced hypoperfusion uses at least 30 mL/kg of crystalloid within the first 3 hours. Balanced crystalloids (LR, Plasma-Lyte) are preferred over 0.9% saline for large-volume resuscitation.

title: Corticosteroids in septic shock
snippet: Hydrocortisone 200 mg/day IV is recommended in septic shock refractory to adequate fluids and vasopressor therapy. Not indicated for sepsis without shock.

title: Sepsis lung-protective ventilation
snippet: For sepsis-induced ARDS, low tidal volume ventilation (6 mL/kg predicted body weight), plateau pressure ≤30 cmH2O, and higher PEEP are recommended. Prone positioning is considered for PaO2/FiO2 <150.

title: Blood transfusion threshold in sepsis
snippet: For hemodynamically stable septic patients, transfuse pRBCs when hemoglobin <7 g/dL. Higher thresholds may apply for active ischemia, hemorrhage, or severe hypoxemia.

title: Vasopressor timing in sepsis
snippet: Vasopressors should be started if MAP <65 mmHg persists after initial fluid bolus. Peripheral norepinephrine may be initiated while central access is obtained.

title: Sepsis glycemic control
snippet: Target blood glucose ≤180 mg/dL in critically ill septic patients. Insulin infusion is initiated when two consecutive glucose values are >180 mg/dL. Avoid hypoglycemia.

title: VTE prophylaxis in ICU
snippet: Pharmacologic VTE prophylaxis (LMWH preferred over UFH) is recommended for critically ill patients in absence of contraindications. Mechanical prophylaxis for patients with active bleeding.

title: Stress ulcer prophylaxis
snippet: Stress ulcer prophylaxis (PPI or H2 blocker) is indicated for ICU patients with risk factors: mechanical ventilation >48h, coagulopathy, or shock.

title: Tension pneumothorax — clinical diagnosis
snippet: Tension pneumothorax is a clinical diagnosis: acute respiratory distress, tracheal deviation away from the affected side, absent breath sounds, hyperresonance, hypotension, distended neck veins. Immediate needle decompression is performed BEFORE imaging in an unstable patient.

title: Needle decompression location
snippet: For adult needle thoracostomy, the preferred site is the 4th or 5th intercostal space, anterior axillary line, using a >5 cm needle-catheter. The traditional 2nd ICS midclavicular line site has higher failure rates in obese patients.

title: Chest tube placement — anatomic landmarks
snippet: Standard chest tube (tube thoracostomy) placement is at the 4th or 5th intercostal space, anterior to the midaxillary line, in the 'safe triangle' (bordered by lateral pectoralis, anterior latissimus, and a horizontal line at the nipple).

title: Massive hemothorax
snippet: Massive hemothorax is defined as >1500 mL initial chest tube output OR ongoing bleeding >200 mL/hr for 2–4 hours. Both are indications for operative thoracotomy.

title: Trauma primary survey ABCDE
snippet: Trauma primary survey follows ABCDE: Airway with cervical spine protection, Breathing and ventilation, Circulation with hemorrhage control, Disability (neurologic status), Exposure/environment. Life-threats are addressed as identified before moving on.

title: Permissive hypotension in trauma
snippet: In non-traumatic-brain-injury hemorrhagic shock, permissive hypotension (SBP target 80–90) may be considered until surgical hemorrhage control. In TBI, MAP ≥80 mmHg is targeted.

title: Massive transfusion protocol
snippet: For massive hemorrhage, 1:1:1 ratio of pRBC:FFP:platelets is standard. TXA (1 g IV over 10 min then 1 g over 8 hr) within 3 hours of injury reduces mortality (CRASH-2).

title: FAST exam in trauma
snippet: FAST (Focused Assessment with Sonography for Trauma) evaluates four windows: pericardial, RUQ (Morison's pouch), LUQ, and suprapubic. Positive in hypotensive blunt trauma prompts operative intervention.

title: Cardiac tamponade — Beck's triad
snippet: Beck's triad of cardiac tamponade: hypotension, muffled heart sounds, jugular venous distension. Pulsus paradoxus and electrical alternans on ECG may be present. Pericardiocentesis is temporizing; definitive is pericardial window or thoracotomy.

title: Cervical spine clearance in trauma
snippet: Cervical spine can be clinically cleared in awake, sober patients without distracting injury who have no midline tenderness, full range of motion, and no neurologic deficit (NEXUS or Canadian C-spine rules). Otherwise, CT is standard.

title: Head injury — Glasgow Coma Scale
snippet: GCS 13–15 mild, 9–12 moderate, ≤8 severe. GCS ≤8 warrants definitive airway (intubation). Serial GCS is more informative than a single value.

title: Pediatric vitals in trauma
snippet: Pediatric heart rate and blood pressure norms are age-dependent. Tachycardia is often the earliest sign of shock in children; hypotension is a late finding. Weight-based dosing and equipment sizing (Broselow) is standard.

title: Pelvic fracture hemorrhage
snippet: Unstable pelvic fractures with hemodynamic instability warrant pelvic binder application, then angioembolization or preperitoneal packing. Retroperitoneal hemorrhage is often occult on FAST.

title: Open fracture management
snippet: Open fractures require early IV antibiotics (cephalosporin ± aminoglycoside based on Gustilo grade), tetanus prophylaxis, irrigation, and operative debridement, ideally within 6 hours.

title: Extubation readiness criteria
snippet: Extubation is considered after successful spontaneous breathing trial (SBT), adequate oxygenation (PaO2/FiO2 >150), stable hemodynamics, intact airway reflexes, appropriate mentation, and manageable secretions. Immediate post-ROSC extubation does not meet these criteria.

title: Ventilator management in ARDS
snippet: Low tidal volume (4–6 mL/kg predicted body weight), plateau pressure ≤30 cmH2O, permissive hypercapnia (pH ≥7.20), and titrated PEEP reduce mortality in ARDS (ARDSNet).
